title: What Happens to People Who Never Hear the Gospel?
excerpt: Christians confess that no one is saved apart from Christ, and most people who ever lived never heard his name. Scripture says who the Judge is and where he sends his church, and it leaves a silence that neither comfort nor fear is allowed to fill.
body:
A woman's grandmother lived her whole life in a village on the other side of the world, prayed every morning in the only faith she had ever been shown, and died without once hearing a sermon about Jesus. The granddaughter is a Christian now, and there are lines in certain hymns she can't sing. A missionary home on leave lies awake doing arithmetic: so many villages, so many years, so many funerals before anyone arrives. A fifteen-year-old asked the question at youth group, was told "that's why we send missionaries," noticed that this was not an answer, and stopped asking.

The skeptic asks it more bluntly. If salvation comes only through Jesus, and most people who have ever lived never heard his name, then it seems that eternity is settled by geography. A God who ran the world that way would be less fair than an ordinary human judge.

That objection deserves its full weight, and the Bible gives it to us in the mouth of Abraham before any skeptic raised it. But some people come to this question because of someone they loved, and for them one thing comes first. No page, preacher or tradition knows another person's heart at the end, and this one will not guess. Judgment belongs to Christ, who wept at a friend's grave. Nothing below speaks of any person's fate. If the grief is too heavy to carry alone, [Find Help](/help) lists places to turn.

## An Old Question

It is sometimes said that only modern people, who know how large the world is, feel this difficulty. The church felt it almost at once.

Around the middle of the second century a Christian teacher named Justin wrote a defense of the faith addressed to the Roman emperor. He knew what a thoughtful pagan would say. If Christ was born only a century and a half ago, then everyone born before him was beyond his reach, and could not fairly be held to account. Justin's answer was that Christ is the Word of God, and that every people has had some share in that Word. He wrote that "those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them." By reasonably he meant in keeping with the Word, the reason of God, whom they did not know by name.

Other Christians have spoken with equal conviction on the other side. The Westminster Confession says that people "not professing the Christian religion" cannot "be saved in any other way whatsoever, be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature." Yet the paragraph just before it leaves a door that the authors did not try to measure. It speaks of infants who die, and then of "all other elect persons who are incapable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the Word," and says that Christ saves them through the Spirit, "who worketh when, and where, and how he pleaseth."

So the two instincts are both old. One says that the Word has never left any people entirely in the dark. The other says that no one is rescued apart from the gospel. Both were written by people who had read the same Bible with care.

## What the Texts Say

Two sentences set the boundary, and neither is soft. Jesus said, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). He said it at a table, on the night before he died, to a frightened disciple who had just asked him, "How can we know the way?" (John 14:5). Peter, standing before the council in Jerusalem, said, "there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). Christians of every tradition take these as they stand. Whoever is saved is saved by Christ. What the two sentences do not say is how much a person must know about him, and it is there that readers divide.

Paul takes up the people who never had the Scriptures in the opening chapters of Romans. He says that God has not left them without knowledge. "His invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse" (Romans 1:20). Read to the end of his sentence, though, and his complaint is not that they lacked information. "Although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him" (Romans 1:21). The light of creation, in Paul's account, is enough to make every person answerable. He never says it is enough to save.

In the next chapter he says how judgment will be measured. "All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law" (Romans 2:12). Those who never had the commandments have a conscience, and their own thoughts "accuse or even excuse them on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus" (Romans 2:15–16). No one in the Bible is condemned for failing to believe a message he never received. The standard is the light a person had, and Paul's judgment on all of us, with every kind of light, is that "all have sinned" (Romans 3:23).

In Athens he spoke to people who had never heard of Moses or of Jesus, and he did not begin with contempt. "I perceive that in every way you are very religious," he said, and he pointed to an altar "To the unknown god" (Acts 17:22–23). Then he said something that bears directly on the charge about geography. God "made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us" (Acts 17:26–27). On Paul's telling, where and when a person is born is no accident that God must work around. It was arranged with that person's seeking in view. He goes on at once: "The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent" (Acts 17:30).

Then there is the chain in Romans 10. "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?" (Romans 10:13–14). Paul wrote it with his own people on his mind, in a section that begins with his "great sorrow and unceasing anguish" (Romans 9:2). He is explaining why preachers must be sent.

One story holds nearly all of this together. Cornelius was a Roman officer, "a devout man who feared God," whose prayers God had heard before he knew anything of Jesus (Acts 10:2). Peter said at his door, "in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him" (Acts 10:35). And yet God did not leave Cornelius as he was. He sent Peter across the country with "a message by which you will be saved" (Acts 11:14).

Taken together, the texts are clear about several things. Salvation is through Christ and no one else. Judgment is just and is measured by the light each person had. God is not far from anyone, and he sends people with the news. What the texts do not give is an account of what he does with each person the news never reached.

## Four Answers

Christians have filled that silence in four ways, and [the site's page on this question](/questions/religions/those-who-never-heard) sets each one out in its holders' terms with the hardest question it faces. They are given here only in outline.

The first holds that a person must hear the gospel and trust Christ in this life. It reads Romans 10 at face value, and adds that no one is condemned for not hearing, only for sin against the light he had, and that God can bring the message to anyone who seeks him, as he did for Cornelius. The second holds that no one is saved apart from Christ, but that his work may reach some who never knew his name and who answered in faith the light God gave them, as it reached Abraham centuries before Bethlehem. The third holds that every person will meet Christ, at death or beyond it, and be able to answer him. The first three are held by Christians who confess the same creeds, and this site takes no side among them.

The fourth is the hope that God will in the end restore everyone. Some early teachers held it, Origen and Gregory of Nyssa among them. The church's councils and confessions have generally not received it, and its hardest question is the plain words of Jesus about a final division. It is stated here without contempt for those who hold it, and the essay on [whether hell is forever](/writing/is-hell-real-and-is-it-forever) treats it at more length.

## The Hunter's Question

Picture a hunter who asks a missionary priest whether he would go to hell if he had never known about God and sin. No, says the priest, not if you did not know. Then why, the hunter asks, did you tell me?

It is the sharpest form of the objection, and it is aimed at the mission itself. If not knowing excuses, the missionary has put people in danger by coming. If it does not excuse, God condemns people over a message nobody brought. The church has felt both edges. William Carey was a shoemaker and village pastor in England when he proposed that Christians had a duty to carry the gospel overseas. As the story has come down, the older minister in the chair called him "a miserable enthusiast" and told him that nothing could be done before another Pentecost. A high doctrine of God's rule had become a reason to stay home.

Carey answered in 1792 with a short book. It is a product of its time, and it speaks of distant peoples in words that are painful to read now. It also contains sentences that cut against his age. Of those peoples he wrote that "they appear to be as capable of knowledge as we are." He called the traffic in human beings on the coast of Africa "the accursed Slave-Trade." And he reminded his readers that the first missionaries had not waited for anyone to become civilized before preaching to "the barbarous Germans and Gauls, and still more barbarous Britons." The English had once been the unreached. He sailed for India the next year and never came home.

What moved him, and what moves the New Testament, is poorly described as a calculation about who is lost. Paul's ambition was "to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named" (Romans 15:20), and the reason he gives is a promise: "Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand" (Romans 15:21). The risen Christ said, "make disciples of all nations" (Matthew 28:19), and gave no report on the fate of the nations to go with it. In John's vision the song of heaven is about what Christ deserves: "by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation" (Revelation 5:9).

That is the answer to the hunter. The gospel is no announcement that makes people guilty who were innocent before. On Paul's account they were already answerable for the light they had, and so was the missionary. It is news of a rescue, and of a Father who was, all along, "not far." A person who believed that would not keep it to himself, whichever of the four answers he held. Each of them leaves the mission standing. The Christian who thinks that some may be saved without hearing still has Cornelius to reckon with. God thought it worth sending a man two days' travel so that one devout soldier could know the name of the one he had been seeking.

There is a word here, too, for the missionary who cannot sleep. The arithmetic of villages was never yours to carry. Jesus said, "I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also" (John 10:16), and the verb is his. When Jonah sulked outside Nineveh, God asked him whether he should not pity "that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left" (Jonah 4:11). The missionary in that book is the one who had to be persuaded. God was already there.

## What We Have Done

We have handled this question badly in two directions.

We have spoken of the dead of other nations with a certainty Scripture never gave us. We have turned them into figures on a fundraising chart. As this site's history course tells it, the missionary century moved on imperial rails. The treaties that ended the Opium Wars wrote toleration of Christian missions into the settlement, so that the faith arrived in China in company with a drug most missionaries despised, and many of them shared their era's contempt for the people they had come to serve. We told the world that God loved it in a tone that made the world doubt it.

And we have done the opposite. Many of us have settled into a vague confidence that everything will come out right for everyone, and we have found it very convenient, because it asks nothing of us. That is the old minister's reply to Carey, said more gently. It is seldom the fruit of study. Mostly it is a way of not having to cross the street, much less the ocean.

There is a third thing, and it concerns the person asking. The Bible's warnings on this subject are not aimed at the grandmother in the village. Paul's argument in Romans 2 is addressed to the religious reader who has the Scriptures and sits in judgment on everyone else. Jesus said that the servant who did not know his master's will "will receive a light beating," and then added, "Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required" (Luke 12:48). Nearly everyone who asks what becomes of those who never heard has heard. Scripture says a great deal about that person, and it is not reassuring.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess that there is one God and "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5), and that whoever is saved is saved by him, by grace. They confess that God "desires all people to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4), that he will judge the world with justice, and that he has sent his church to every nation. These belong to the faith itself.

How the one Savior reaches those who never heard of him is a question of the second order. Christians who share the creeds answer it differently, and no creed decides it.

What has become of any particular person is not given to us at all. "The secret things belong to the LORD our God" (Deuteronomy 29:29).

When Abraham learned that judgment was coming on a city, he stood in front of God and argued. "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25). God did not rebuke him for asking. He let him ask six times. Abraham was never shown how the judgment would be worked out. He was shown who the Judge was. That is still all anyone has been shown, with one addition Abraham did not have. The Judge has since been seen. He came within reach, was himself condemned by a court, and prayed for the people who killed him.

For the granddaughter and her hymns, that is not an answer. It tells her whose hands the question is in, and the question stays open.

*"Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?"* (Genesis 18:25)

*"Yet he is actually not far from each one of us."* (Acts 17:27)
